chapter_theme: Songs at Kodunkundram (கொடுங்குன்றம்): the poet asks Murugan to look on his crippled service, bent by women, and promises never to forget the dancing feet even as the body perishes in the sea of lust; one song's praise is a long drum-syllable battle.
structure_note: 621 is a short song; 622 is one of the longest in the book, with its confession built on the image of breasts as war elephants and its praise almost wholly drum syllables.

621.reading: The poet says that through eyes where Kama's five arrows dwell, through breasts like golden hills and pots, and through women who grow angry and exact payment in public, his service is crippled, and asks whether Murugan will not see it and be glad today. The praise hears the bees humming in the dense groves and names the Lord who dwells on the rich, steep hill of Kodunkundram.
621.nuance: முடங்கும் என்றன் தொண்டு: service is not abandoned but bent and crippled, and the plea is only that the Lord look at it. மன்றம் கண்டும் தண்டும் பெண்கள் may mean women who take a man to the public hall and exact money; the reading is unsure.

622.reading: The poet describes breasts as rutting war elephants that burst their bodices, run with musk, break the pearl chains that bind them, crush their keepers, shake even Kama and three-eyed Siva and swallow young men's lives; then the women who set a price in public, their embraces, poisonous carp eyes and kisses, and the net of lovemaking in which he sinks into a dark sea of senses. He vows that even when this hut of the body, a shirt for the senses, perishes, he will not forget Murugan's dancing feet at Kodunkiri. The praise is almost all drum syllables and a battlefield of vultures, Bhairavas bathing in blood and demons beheaded.
622.nuance: கொங்கை யானை, breast-elephant, is sustained for many lines, with chains (நிகளம்), goad (அங்குசம்) and keepers (பாகர்). பொதுவில் விலையிடு மகளிர் are women who set their price publicly. இந்திரிய சட்டைக் குரம்பை, the body as a hut that is the senses' shirt, is the image of what perishes; the plea is not to escape but not to forget (மறந்திடேனே).

links.note: 622 calls the body a hut that is the senses' shirt (இந்திரிய சட்டைக் குரம்பை) and vows not to forget the feet even when it perishes. Tirumanthiram 312 uses the same word for the body, the hut that does not stay (நில்லாக் குரம்பை), and says those who think it lasting cannot see the Lord. 622 is the right response to the fact 312 states.

622 vows that even at the moment the body perishes (குரம்பை அழி பொழுதினிலும்) he will not forget the dancing feet (மறந்திடேனே). Tirumanthiram 176, on the plainest reading, says that when life leaves the body there is no way to fight, but Death's messengers do not come near one who thinks of the Lord (அண்ணலை எண்ணும்). Both make remembrance at the death-hour the defence; 176's construction is uncertain.
